figure: Figure 9.3 — The payload path is not the bootstrap path
issue: The dashed red setup arrows are thin and low-contrast relative to the solid black payload arrows. In grayscale they become mid-gray dashed lines, and at print size the connection from the setup box to ProcessGroupNCCL/ProcessGroupXCCL is easy to miss.
evidence: The legend distinguishes “Payload / execution” as a solid black arrow and “Control / setup” as a dashed red arrow. The dashed red lines run from the top setup box down the outside of the framework-backend boxes; they are visibly lighter and thinner than the solid arrows.
acceptance_test: Increase the dashed setup-line weight or contrast, or add a short direct label on each dashed connector (“setup only”), and inspect a grayscale print proof to confirm the dashed path remains immediately visible.

issue: Panel A labels the all-reduce communication step in a floating red dashed box below the GPUs, but no arrows connect the GPUs to that box or the box to “full output.” The communication step is therefore visually detached from the computation it summarizes.
evidence: Panel A shows GPU 0 and GPU 1 with weight shards W0 and W1, then a red dashed box reading “all-reduce partial sums → full output” beneath them. There are no connector arrows from the GPU boxes into or out of the all-reduce box.

figure: Figure 10.1 — Three parallelism patterns, one per panel
issue: Panel B says “idle (bubble) at fill/drain — pipeline-wide” but the diagram does not visually encode the bubble. The panel shows only three sequential stage boxes and arrows; the key pipeline-parallel cost is asserted in text rather than shown.

figure: Figure 11.1 — Discrete vs continuous batching
issue: The green admission events are drawn as finite-width blocks, and the annotation arrow 'a finishing sequence frees its slot immediately' points at one of those green blocks. This conflates the freeing event (end of a blue sequence) with the admission event (start of the next sequence) and visually implies that admission consumes decode-step time.
evidence: Legend: 'admission event (backfill)' is a green rectangle; caption calls it an 'admission tick'; the arrow from 'a finishing sequence frees its slot immediately' terminates on a green bar, not on the end of the preceding blue block or the freed slot. The green bars have visible width along the time axis.
acceptance_test: Redraw admission as a zero-width vertical tick at the slot boundary (or explicitly label it as instantaneous), and point the 'frees its slot' arrow to the end of the blue sequence / the freed slot, not to the admission tick. Verify that a reader cannot infer that admission takes a decode step.

figure: Figure 11.1 — Discrete vs continuous batching
issue: The legend distinguishes 'sequence in flight' (blue) from 'admission event' (green) by hue alone. In grayscale the two colors have nearly identical luminance, so the narrow green admission bars become visually indistinguishable from blue sequence blocks.
evidence: Legend uses solid blue for sequence and solid green for admission; no pattern or shape difference. Approximate luminance of the blue and green fills is very close, and the green bars are small, making the distinction fragile in grayscale or for color-vision differences.
acceptance_test: Add a non-color distinction (hatching, outline, or a clearly different luminance) to the admission event, and verify the figure in grayscale at print size. The reader must still distinguish sequence blocks from admission events without color.

figure: Figure 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue: The prefill boxes are labeled 'PREFFILL' (double F) in both panels. This is a visible spelling error in a key figure label.
evidence: Panel A red box reads 'PREFFILL 4 GPUs'; panel B red box reads 'PREFFILL 8 GPUs'. The correct term used throughout the prose is 'prefill'.
acceptance_test: Correct both labels to 'PREFILL' and re-render the figure.

figure: Figure 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue: Panel A draws a single thick KV arrow between the 4-GPU prefill group and the 4-GPU decode group, labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'. The single-arrow visual suggests one shared 450 GB/s link, while the prose and caveat treat the case as four per-GPU links whose aggregate is 1.8 TB/s. The figure's caveat then says '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link above', which is true per link but can be misread as saying the panel-A configuration cannot absorb the aggregate load.
evidence: Panel A: one arrow labeled '450 GB/s per GPU per direction'; note 'square = one GPU'. Prose Note 11.3-1: 'the panel's 4-way shard would be 35 ÷ (4 × 450) ≈ 0.02 s' and '4 decode GPUs × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s aggregate ingress absorbs the 1.4 TB/s'. Figure caveat: '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link above.'
acceptance_test: Either draw four per-GPU KV links (or a labeled aggregate '4 × 450 GB/s = 1.8 TB/s') in panel A, or revise the arrow label and caveat to distinguish single-link capacity from aggregate capacity. Verify that a reader cannot conclude panel A is infeasible at 40 req/s when the prose says the aggregate is feasible but tight.

figure: Figure 11.4 — Device visibility is not a validated serving path
issue: The figure is text-dense, and the smallest text — especially the multi-line 'Kernels / runtime' descriptions and the qualification-gate requirements — appears below the book's 8 pt figure-annotation floor at print size.

figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue: The caption’s reduction-factor calculation is dimensionally ambiguous. It gives “M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16)”, but M in the formula is an element count, while “192 KB of fp16” is a byte capacity. If a reader substitutes 192 KB directly, M/d² ≈ 12, not 6. The printed 6× is correct only if M is read as ~96K fp16 elements.
evidence: Caption: “a reduction factor of M/d² (≈6× at d = 128, M ≈ 192 KB of fp16)”. 192 KB of fp16 = 98,304 elements; 98,304 / 128² ≈ 6. But 192,000 / 128² ≈ 11.7. The caption does not state that M is in elements.
acceptance_test: The caption states M in the same units as d², e.g. “M ≈ 96K fp16 elements (192 KB)” or “M/d² ≈ 6× at d = 128, M ≈ 96K elements”, so the arithmetic is unambiguous.

figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue: The AFTER panel’s phrase “no single global K/V pass” is ambiguous. It can be read as “there is no global K/V pass at all”, whereas the intended meaning is “there is no single global pass over all K/V for all queries; K/V is re-read per tile”. The caption clarifies, but the diagram label itself is misleading.
evidence: AFTER panel: “K/V reused per tile — no single global K/V pass; no L×L intermediate at HBM”. Caption: “it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks”.
acceptance_test: Rephrase to “K/V re-read per tile; not a single global pass” or “no single global K/V pass over all queries”, so the label cannot be read as denying all global K/V reads.

figure: Figure 18.1 — Model-routing decision tree
issue: The Cost/SLO gate is semantically under-specified. A single 'yes' arrow splits to both Frontier and Small gen, with the label 'yes → SLO: frontier cost: small'. The diagram does not show the decision rule that distinguishes Frontier from Small gen, so the reader cannot tell whether the gate is choosing by SLO, cost, or both.

acceptance_test: Replace the single 'yes' branch with two explicit branches (e.g., 'SLO requires frontier → Frontier' and 'cost-sensitive → Small gen'), or add a decision diamond with the actual criteria. A reader should be able to explain the Frontier-vs-Small-gen choice from the figure alone.

figure: Figure 19.1 — The agent loop: a four-state machine
issue: The diagram contradicts the caption on what terminates the loop at the limit. The caption says 'a turn/token budget check — not the model's judgment — ends the loop at the limit', but the 'limit hit' arrow originates from the 'Decide' state, which is labeled 'check' and 'resolved?'. This visually implies the model's Decide state determines the limit hit.

The figure must not imply that the model's judgment enforces the hard limit.

figure: Figure 19.2 — Token growth vs resulting KV growth across agent turns
issue: The caption's final sentence groups prefix caching with fleet sizing and FP8 KV as a response to KV footprint growth, but the same caption correctly says prefix caching 'does not by itself reduce the request's own KV-resident context'.
